Broken Chord Paper Folding

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: A triangle sits on a circle, and a crease cuts through it. Move the corners and watch one corner flip across the crease; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the blue points A, B and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick Show hint to draw the crease and the flipped point; the other boxes add more marks.

Drag A, B or C, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

This is Archimedes' broken chord theorem, told as a paper fold. The surprising part is that the point where the crease lands explains a length that looks as if it has nothing to do with folding.

Find the halfway point of the arc

The three corners lie on their circumcircle. The point P is the midpoint of the arc from A through C to B: it is equally far from A and from B, and it sits on C's side of the chord AB. The applet finds it by crossing the circle with the perpendicular bisector of AB and keeping the crossing on that side.

From P drop a perpendicular to the longer of AC and BC; its foot is M. When AC is longer, the theorem says AM = MC + CB — M cuts the bent path A–C–B into two equal lengths. If BC is longer, swap A and B and the same statement holds. The logic test checked both cases over 1,964 triangles: the largest difference between the two halves was 3 × 10−10 board units, and M always fell on the side it was supposed to.

Unfold the paper

Now fold the picture along the line PC. The reflection of B in that crease is the orange point F. A fold keeps distances, so CF = CB, and F lands exactly on the line from A through C, beyond C. The reason is that PC is the angle bisector of the angle between CB and the extension of CA: the angles marked in the page's proof come in pairs, with α + γ = β. All of those angle pairs and the crease's bisector property were measured in the logic test; the largest angle mismatch was 5 × 10−11 radians.

Why the two halves match

Because P is the arc midpoint, AP = PB; the fold gives PB = PF, so triangle APF is isosceles. The line PM is its altitude, so it also cuts AF in half: AM = MF. But F lies beyond C and CF = CB, so MF = MC + CF = MC + CB. Put the two equalities together and you have AM = MC + CB, exactly the broken chord theorem. Across the 1,964 tested triangles the largest error in AM − (MC + CB) was 3 × 10−10.

Tick Extra fold to reflect the other end instead: the image G gives a second isosceles triangle, obtained from the first by turning the paper around P. The applet's own "distance less than one board unit" fallback is kept: if P and C almost coincide it reflects in the point P rather than in the line PC.

Tick Show hint and drag C around the circle: the crease swings, but the two halves stay equal. Then drag A almost onto B to see the picture stop being drawn.
